Splitting pairs
Since 2000, Nvidia has split its stock six times, an average of once every four years. The last split was in 2024, so that indicates that, on average, we should expect a split in 2028. But averages can be deceiving.
Nvidia's splits have generally come in pairs, with longer gaps between splits. Its first 2-for-1 stock split was in June 2000, and was quickly followed by another 2-for-1 split in September 2001. In a 2-for-1 split, the company issues each stockholder two new shares for every old share they hold, but the share price is cut in half, so while the number of shares doubles, the total value of each investor's position doesn't change.

Image source: Nvidia. After the September 2001 split, it was almost five years before another one, which took the form of a third 2-for-1 split in April 2006. That was again followed fairly rapidly by another split in September 2007. This time, however, the split was a 3-for-2 split, meaning that each investor's share count was increased by 1.5 times instead of doubling.

The final two splits occurred in July 2021, when the stock split 4-for-1, quadrupling the share count, and the most recent 2024 split, which was a massive 10-for-1 split. For those keeping track, that means investors who owned a single share of Nvidia stock before June 2000 now own 480 shares.
Because we just had a pair of (large) stock splits in the recent past, Nvidia would seem less likely to offer one in the near future, but there's one more factor to consider: share price.

Image source: Nvidia. Why split now?
One big reason a company splits its stock price is that the price of a single share has become so expensive that it's out of reach for many retail investors. Of course, with fractional shares -- buying less than a full share of stock -- now an option at many brokerages, that's not necessarily a barrier to owning a pricey stock.

Story Continues

Nvidia's stock prices at the time of its first four splits were well below its current $180 per share, ranging from about $50 per share in 2007 to about $142 per share in 2000. However, its last two split prices were much higher: about $751 per share in 2021 and $1,200 per share in 2024. Currently, Nvidia's stock is trading for about $180 per share, so it seems unlikely the company will split its stock until it's increased at least a little bit more from here.

In this article NVIDIA no longer sells chips so much as entire AI factories, and the buyers of those factories now stretch far beyond the hyperscalers. Our work on the companies doing the buying points to a larger and longer buildout than the market is pricing, along with a sharper competitive fight and a growing financing role that every shareholder should understand.
In February, we published a model of Nebius that had the company reaching roughly 2.65 gigawatts of connected capacity by 2029. Four months later, contracted power had already passed 3.5 gigawatts, NVIDIA had invested $2 billion in the company, and Meta had signed an agreement worth up to $27 billion. We tore the model down and rebuilt it from the physical layer up.
The capital plan told the story. Our February work implied roughly $69 billion of Nebius spending from 2026 through 2029. The June rebuild carried $175 billion from 2026 through 2030. Our current owned-growth model carries $274.9 billion from 2026 through 2030, excluding partner-owned and replacement spending.
The same pattern has repeated across the AI infrastructure companies we cover. Each time we go back to the site maps, the contracts, and the funding stacks, the equipment bill gets bigger. A large share of every one of those bills lands in one place: NVIDIA's income statement.
This forecast reads the AI buildout from the supplier's side of the invoice. Before we get to the numbers, it helps to see the whole company clearly, since most of the debate about NVIDIA comes down to which parts of it people are looking at.
The Company in One Picture
NVIDIA reported $96.2 billion of revenue in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, more than double the year before, and guided the next quarter to $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, per its Q2 release . Data Center produced $89.0 billion of that quarter. Gaming, professional graphics, automotive, and robotics, reported within Edge Computing, produced $7.2 billion, about 7.5% of quarterly revenue. Data Center now dominates the business.
Gross margin ran at 75%, and roughly two-thirds of every revenue dollar reached operating profit. Hardware companies rarely look like this. NVIDIA earns software-like margins on physical equipment, and the question of how long it can keep doing so sits underneath every serious debate about the stock.
The company now reports Data Center revenue in two groups. Hyperscale covers the largest cloud and internet companies. AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise, or ACIE, captures a broad channel serving independent AI clouds, sovereign projects and enterprises. Its end demand also includes frontier labs and hyperscalers renting through those clouds. Buyer groups and reporting categories are different classifications.
In the second quarter, Hyperscale produced $48.7 billion and ACIE $40.3 billion, per the CFO commentary . ACIE grew 25% from the prior quarter and 138% from the year before. Management now expects the non-hyperscale side to reach about half of Data Center revenue.
The split is the single most important fact for anyone new to the company. Nearly half of NVIDIA's largest business already comes from customers who sit outside the hyperscaler spending totals most investors track.
Two Desks, One Invoice
Sit in on most investment conversations about AI infrastructure and you will hear two arguments that rarely meet.
At one desk, investors ask how CoreWeave, Nebius, and IREN will finance their next wave of data centers. At another, they ask how NVIDIA can keep growing when Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta are already spending at record levels and designing their own chips. The first group worries the buyers are overextended. The second worries the buyers are running out, or leaving.
Both conversations are about the same invoice. The equipment bill that creates a financing problem for a cloud operator is a revenue line for its supplier, and the two debates belong together.
The Street mostly prices NVIDIA from the top down. It totals the capital budgets of the largest clouds, applies a share for NVIDIA, and asks how much higher the total can go. Moody's, for instance, tracks spending at Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, and CoreWeave at roughly $785 billion in 2026 , closing in on $1 trillion in 2027. Those are enormous numbers, and they still leave out most of the independent clouds, sovereign projects, and enterprise buyers we model.
The top-down frame also tends to run behind. Before NVIDIA's August earnings call, the average analyst expected about 44% revenue growth in fiscal 2028. Management then guided to roughly 70%, and our own fiscal 2027 estimate of $409.8 billion already sat above the roughly $396 billion consensus cited at the time.
None of that surprised us. Our CoreWeave model, published in August, already had capital spending rising from $33.0 billion in 2026 to $44.1 billion in 2027. Our June Nebius rebuild had 2027 spending climbing 58% from 2026. The buyers were telling us the year ahead would be bigger than consensus assumed before NVIDIA said so itself.
Our view is direct. The purchasing base for NVIDIA's equipment is broader, deeper, and longer-lived than a hyperscaler spending screen can capture, and NVIDIA is capturing more of every dollar spent inside each data center. We believe the shares are undervalued as a result.
